title: Confirmation Bias
shortDefinition: The natural tendency to search for, interpret, and remember information that confirms pre-existing beliefs, while ignoring contradictory facts.
dailyExample: Believing 'Nobody at work likes me,' and fixating on the one colleague who didn't smile this morning while completely overlooking the three people who greeted you warmly.
psychologyTheory: Described by Peter Wason (1960). The brain seeks cognitive efficiency. Finding affirming evidence requires less metabolic energy than revising core mental frameworks.
inTherapy: We challenge cognitive biases by asking for contradictory evidence. Clients learn to look for 'disconfirming data' before cementing painful assumptions.
practicalTakeaway: Next time you form a harsh conclusion about someone or yourself, actively challenge your brain: 'What is one piece of evidence that contradicts this narrative?'
